plan.chapterName: Anton, Bivens, and Davis. Calculus, 10th Edition, Figure 14.2.9
plan.contextChunk: This figure is part of a worked example asking to evaluate the double integral of (2x - y^2) over the triangular region R enclosed between y = -x + 1, y = x + 1, and y = 3. The figure shows the triangular region R in the xy-plane with vertices at (-2, 3), (0, 1), and (2, 3); the bounding lines y = 3 (top), y = -x + 1 (lower left), and y = x + 1 (lower right) are labeled. The y-axis divides R into two sub-regions: R1 (shaded blue, left half) and R2 (shaded yellow, right half), each with a red vertical strip indicating the direction of inner integration. The figure illustrates the decomposition of R into two type-I sub-regions required when the lower boundary changes expression across the y-axis.

interactionPlan.concept: A triangular region may require two Type I integrals because its lower boundary changes at x = 0, while the same region can be described as one Type II integral using horizontal slices.

interactions.teaches: The learner sees that a vertical slice has one lower boundary formula on the left of the y-axis and a different lower boundary formula on the right, so the Type I description must split into two pieces.
interactions.label: Edit lower boundary equations

interactions.teaches: The learner understands that changing the order of integration changes the slicing direction and can turn a split Type I description into a single Type II description.
interactions.label: Slice description

demo_steps.title: Start with the triangular region
demo_steps.narration: The region R is bounded above by y = 3 and below by two different slanted lines meeting at (0, 1). The y-axis naturally divides the triangle into R1 and R2.

demo_steps.title: Use vertical slices
demo_steps.narration: A vertical strip in R1 runs from y = -x + 1 up to y = 3, while a vertical strip in R2 runs from y = x + 1 up to y = 3. Because the lower boundary changes at x = 0, the Type I integral is written as two integrals.

demo_steps.title: Edit the lower boundaries
demo_steps.narration: Changing either lower-boundary equation redraws that side of the triangle and updates the corresponding limits. This makes the split at x = 0 visible as a consequence of having two different lower boundary formulas.

demo_steps.title: Switch to horizontal slices
demo_steps.narration: With horizontal slices, one strip crosses the entire region from the left line x = 1 - y to the right line x = y - 1. The region can now be described with one Type II integral instead of two Type I integrals.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The need to split an iterated integral depends on the slicing direction: vertical slices see two different lower boundaries, but horizontal slices see one continuous left-to-right interval.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Draw a clean xy-plane with the y-axis passing through the middle of an inverted triangular region and the x-axis below it. The triangle has a flat top boundary y = 3 from x = -2 to x = 2, a left descending boundary y = -x + 1, and a right ascending boundary y = x + 1 meeting at the bottom vertex on the y-axis. Use a thick cyan outline for the triangle. In Type I view, shade the left half light blue and label it R1, shade the right half light yellow and label it R2, and place one red vertical strip in each half. Show Type I limits and the split integral nearby. In Type II view, show the full triangle as one region with horizontal blue strips and display the single set of limits 1 <= y <= 3, 1 - y <= x <= y - 1. Keep equation labels near their corresponding boundaries and update boundary curves, shading, and limit readouts when the equation inputs change.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- equation_input for the two lower boundary equations: two fields pre-filled with "-x + 1" (left, for R1) and "x + 1" (right, for R2); when the learner edits either, the corresponding boundary line redraws, the shaded sub-regions R1 and R2 update, and the inner integral limits display — shows directly how the lower boundary formula changing expression at x=0 is what forces the decomposition into two sub-integrals
- toggle between Type I (vertical slices, R1 + R2 split with red strips) and Type II (horizontal slices, single region with blue horizontal strips and limits x from -(y-1) to (y-1)) — teaches that switching integration order eliminates the need to decompose R
